There are many different varieties of [[pasta]].{{sfn|Zanini De Vita|2009|page=xiv}} It may be long ({{lang|it|pasta lunga}}) or short ({{lang|it|pasta corta}}). It may have a simple shape like a thin cylinder (spaghetti), a sheet (lasagna), a tube (penne), or a grain, or be complex and three-dimensional. It may be stuffed or not. It may be boiled, then served drained (''pastasciutta''), cooked in broth (''pasta in brodo''), baked (''pasta in forno''). Some varieties are ubiquitous, others are unknown outside their region of origin.

Names vary by region, by language, and by manufacturer: "one man's {{lang|it|gnocchetto}} can be another's {{lang|it|strascinato}}".{{sfn|Zanini De Vita|2009|page=xviii}} For example, cut [[rotelle]] are also called {{lang|it|ruote}} in Italy and 'wagon wheels' in the United States. Manufacturers and cooks often invent new shapes of pasta, or may rename pre-existing shapes.

[[Italian language|Italian]] pasta names often end with the [[Gender (linguistics)|masculine]] [[Number (linguistics)|plural]] [[diminutive]] [[suffix]]es {{lang|it|-ini, -elli, -illi, -etti}} or the feminine plurals {{lang|it|-ine, -elle}}, etc., all conveying the sense of {{gloss|little}}; or with the [[augmentative]] suffixes {{lang|it|-oni, -one}}, meaning {{gloss|large}}. Other suffixes like {{lang|it|-otti}} {{gloss|largish}}, and {{lang|it|-acci}} {{gloss|rough, badly made}}, may also occur.

Long pasta may be made by [[Food extrusion|extrusion]] or rolling and cutting.{{Clear}}
